findings.title: Backup code can be used to log in without the account password
findings.body: The credentials provider only verifies the password when `credentials.totpCode` is empty (`if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` a few lines above). The new backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is true, regardless of `totpCode`. An attacker can therefore POST `email` + empty `password` + any garbage `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") + a valid `backupCode` and be logged in without ever proving knowledge of the password. Unlike a TOTP code, a backup code is static and never expires, so a single leaked/stolen backup code becomes a standalone, long-lived credential for the account. The backup-code check should require a successful password verification (or at minimum must not be reachable on the password-skipping path).

findings.title: Backup code consumption is a read-modify-write and can be raced
findings.body: The code list is read in the earlier `prisma.user.findUnique`, mutated in memory (`backupCodes[index] = null`) and written back with a full `update`. Two concurrent login attempts that both read the same ciphertext can both succeed with the *same* backup code, and the second write will also resurrect codes consumed by the first attempt (last write wins). Backup codes are meant to be single use; this allows replay of a code that was already spent. Consumption needs to be atomic (e.g. a transaction with a conditional update / optimistic version check on the stored value).

findings.title: Backup codes are stored reversibly encrypted instead of hashed
findings.body: Backup codes are persisted as `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`, i.e. recoverable plaintext for anyone with the DB dump and the shared app encryption key (the same key used for many other things and typically present in the app environment). Because a backup code bypasses 2FA entirely, these should be stored as one-way hashes and compared by hashing the submitted value, so a database/key compromise does not immediately yield usable 2FA-bypass credentials. Additionally each code carries only 40 bits of entropy (`crypto.randomBytes(5)`), which is low for a credential that is checked by an endpoint reachable by unauthenticated callers.

findings.title: onEnable() is now deferred to the Close button, so dismissing the dialog desyncs UI and loses the codes
findings.body: Previously `onEnable()` was invoked as soon as the enable request succeeded; now it is only called from the "Close" button on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step. If the user dismisses the dialog with ESC/outside click/X after 2FA was already enabled server side, the parent is never notified: the two-factor switch stays in the "off" state even though 2FA is enabled on the account, and the backup codes are gone forever (there is no regenerate path). Notify the parent as soon as the server confirms enablement, and/or handle `onOpenChange` on this step.

findings.title: "missing_backup_codes" tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such option exists
findings.body: The message "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." is shown (login page and disable modal) when `user.backupCodes` is null. Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has null `backupCodes` (the migration does not backfill), and this PR adds no UI to generate codes for an already-enabled 2FA account — codes are only created by `totp/setup`, which rejects users with `twoFactorEnabled` true. Users following this instruction will find nothing in settings; the only route is disabling 2FA (which requires a working authenticator) and re-enabling. Either add a regeneration flow or change the message to reflect reality.

findings.title: resetState leaves stale backup codes and leaks the blob object URL
findings.body: `resetState()` clears only `password`, `errorMessage` and `step`. `backupCodes` and `backupCodesUrl` are kept, so after closing and reopening the dialog the previously generated codes and download URL remain in component state (and are still reachable by the download anchor until a new setup overwrites them). The object URL created with `URL.createObjectURL` is only revoked on the next successful setup, so dialogs that are cancelled leak the blob for the lifetime of the document. Clear `backupCodes` and revoke/clear `backupCodesUrl` in `resetState` (and on unmount).

findings.title: No test covers the actual backup-code authentication paths
findings.body: The only added coverage exercises the download/copy/close buttons on the new setup screen. The security-critical new logic — logging in with a backup code via the credentials provider (including single-use consumption) and disabling 2FA with a backup code in `totp/disable.ts` — has no test at all, as the added TODO acknowledges. Given this code path can authenticate a user, at least one test that logs in with a stored code and asserts the code cannot be reused should be added.

findings.title: Assertion on the 2FA switch is a no-op and was documented rather than fixed
findings.body: `expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` asserts on the returned Promise, which is always truthy, so the first test never verifies that 2FA was actually enabled (the added FIXME admits this). Use `await expect(locator).toBeChecked()` or the `[data-state="checked"]` selector used in the second test so the test can actually fail.

findings.title: Unvalidated/unguarded backup code handling can throw an unhandled 500
findings.body: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, key))` and `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` are not guarded: if the stored ciphertext was written with a different `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (decrypt/parse throws) or if a client sends a non-string `backupCode` (e.g. a number or object), the handler throws a raw exception and returns an unhandled 500 instead of a meaningful error code. Validate the request body type and wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch returning a defined ErrorCode.

findings.title: tabIndex={-1} makes the password reveal toggle unreachable by keyboard
findings.body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from the tab order globally for every `PasswordField` in the app, so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer toggle password visibility (the `sr-only` label and tooltip become unreachable). If the intent was only to keep focus out of the way in the 2FA modals, this should not be applied to the shared component unconditionally.
